skeleton:
Black Pudding and Fried Egg Stack

British · Easy · Serves 2

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The vertical fry-up: fried bread, black pudding, egg, and brown sauce built into a two-tier stack you cut through with the side of a fork. It is the café's answer to the plated full English when the counter is crowded — everything in one column, every layer distinct, the yolk running down through the strata like sauce that knows its job. Four ingredients, fifteen minutes, and more theatre per calorie than any flat plate.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The stack (per serving, ×2)

Seasoning and finish

- **Order matters for warmth:** the stack builds bottom-up in the pan's own sequence — bread fries first and holds, pudding sears next, egg lands last. No oven holding needed; the stack assembles hot in under a minute. - **A serrated or sharp knife for the finished stack** — you cut through crust, crust, and white in one clean press, not a saw.

Black Pudding and Fried Egg Stack

Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 15 minutes · Total: 20 minutes · Serves 2

Ingredients

The stack (per serving, ×2)

  • 1 slice (60 g) thick white bread, fried
  • 2 thick slices (150 g) black pudding, 1.5 cm each
  • 1 large egg (55 g)
  • 5 g butter, for the egg
  • 2 tsp (10 g) brown breakfast sauce

Seasoning and finish

  • 1 g black pepper
  • 5 g chives, snipped (optional)

Instructions

  1. **Fry the bread, 3 minutes.** Fry the bread in a lightly oiled pan over medium heat, 90 seconds a side, until golden and crisp-edged. Hold on the plate. Checkpoint — the bread is gold and crusty outside but still bread within — fried, not a crouton.
  2. **Sear the black pudding, 5 minutes.** In the same pan, sear the pudding slices 2–3 minutes a side until dark-crusted and warmed through. Checkpoint — dark crust both faces, slice holding firm, fat beading at the surface.
  3. **The fried egg, 2–3 minutes.** Add the butter to the pan's fat, and when it foams, crack in the egg. Baste the hot fat over the white until set — 2 minutes — yolk liquid. Checkpoint — whites fully set with lacy edges, yolk domed and trembling.
  4. **Stack and sauce.** Bread on the plate, brown sauce spread thinly across its top face, both pudding slices on the sauce, the fried egg crowning the pudding, pepper over. Chives if using. Cut through with a sharp knife at the table — or don't cut, and eat downward. Checkpoint — the stack stands for ten seconds at least (the structural test), and the first cut sends yolk down the pudding's crust to the sauce below — the plate's own architecture doing the plating.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Stack slid overWet egg or greasy layersDrain the egg 3 seconds; tilt the bread to shed excess fat before stacking
Pudding crumbled mid-stackSlices cut thin1.5 cm minimum; thick slices are structural
Bread went cold under the eggAssembled too slowlyThe stack builds in 60 seconds — have everything cooked and at hand first

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **No storage — this is a 20-minute now dish**, eaten standing if the mood takes. - **Variation — the hash brown tier:** a thin hash brown between pudding and egg; the stack gains a third crust and loses none of its stability. - **Variation — the vegetarian stack:** the bubble-and-squeak cake replaces the pudding; same architecture, gentler plate. - **The caf version:** served on a saucer with a mug of tea, eaten at the counter, cut once through the middle and never again discussed.

methodSteps.chefsNote: the stack's stability comes from its sauce layer doing double duty: the brown sauce is a thin, tacky adhesive between bread and pudding, gripping the crust where butter would slide. Spread it to the bread's edges, not the centre — the perimeter bond is what stops the upper layers shearing sideways at the first cut. And cut with the serrated knife's own weight, no downward push: a pushed cut flattens the stack and squirts the yolk out the back.
